16395.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse forkr (“boathook; pole, staff”), itself borrowed from Latin furca (“two-pronged fork, pitchfork; fork-shaped prop or pole”).
The further origin of the Latin word is uncertain. It has been connected with Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰerk(ʷ)- (“fork”) and *ǵʰerg(ʷ)- (“fork”), although the consonant development is problematic. Alternatively, it may be related to Proto-Germanic *furkaz (“stake, stick, pole, post”) and *firkalaz (“stake, stick, pole, post”), ultimately associated with Proto-Indo-European *perg- (“pole, post”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk fork (“stick; forked stick;  / Borrowed from English fork (“branching; independently developed copy of software; split in a blockchain”). Ultimately etymologically related to the native noun in Etymology 1 through Latin furca (“fork, pitchfork”).

1000459.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Serbo-Croatian Hèrcegovina, from hèrceg (“duke”) + -ov (“possessive suffix”) + -ina (“suffix forming names of territories”), literally “the duke's land”.
The title hèrceg (“duke”) was borrowed from Hungarian herceg (“duke”), from Middle High German herzog (“duke”), ultimately from Old High German herizogo (“army leader, duke”). The latter was originally a compound meaning “army leader”.
The region was named after the lands of Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, who assumed the title herceg in 1448, initially styling himself duke of Hum and the coast and subsequently duke of Saint

1000971.etyen:
Learned borrowing from Latin Iūliānus (“Roman personal name”), shortened by the loss of the Latin nominative ending -us. The Latin name was derived from Latin Iūlius (“Julius”) with the relational suffix -ānus (“belonging to, connected with”), and originally denoted someone belonging to or descended from the Roman gens Julia. The ultimate origin of Iūlius is uncertain; see Julius.
Compare Danish Julian, Swedish Julian, German Julian, English Julian, French Julien, Spanish Julián and Italian Giuliano (“male given name”).

1001995.etyen:
A former Norwegian dialectal variant of Einar (“male given name”), particularly associated with the area traditionally described as Nordafjells.
Inherited from Old Norse Einarr, probably formed from *ainaz (“one, single”), from *h₁óynos (“one, single”), and *harjaz (“warrior”), from *kóryos (“war, troops”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *ker- (“army”), literally “one warrior”.
Compare Icelandic Einar, Faroese Einar, Swedish Enar and Danish Ener (“male given name”).

1002763.etyen:
Clipping of Bodil (“female given name”). The source name Bodil was Danish Bodil, ultimately from Old Norse Bóthildr, a female given name formed from bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) and hildr (“battle, fight”).
The forms Bol and Boel were especially used in Norway in the 18th and 19th centuries and could be used interchangeably for the same person; both were traditionally pronounced as one syllable.
Compare Swedish Bol (“female given name”).

1004043.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse búi (“dweller, inhabitant; farmer”), from búa (“to live, dwell; farm”), from Proto-Germanic *būaną (“to dwell, live, cultivate”). The suffix originally denotes someone who lives or dwells in a place, and is used in inhabitant names formed from place names or landscape terms.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -bu, Swedish -bo and Danish -bo (“inhabitant-forming suffix”).

1005067.etyen:
From Botolv (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Botolf”.
The given name Botolv goes back to Old Norse Bótólfr, a male given name formed from bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) and úlfr (“wolf”), literally “remedy-wolf”. The first element is from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“improvement, betterment; recompense, atonement”), while the second is from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz (“wolf”).
